To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
renal mechanosensors, which are located in the renal pelvis, are impaired in heart failure due to angiotensin II inhibiting substance P release from renal mechanosensatory nerves.
renal mechanosensors in heart failure are less sensitive to renal pelvic pressure, and the impairment is mediated by endogenous ANG II.

in rats with heart failure, the responsiveness of the renal mechanosensors that are responsible for the release of the peptide transmitter substance P is reduced, which may be a cause for sodium retention in heart failure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the renal pelvis in the regulation of renal function in health and disease.
the role of ANG II on the release of substance P in renal pelvic nerves in normal and CHF rats.
the role of renal mechanosensation in renal function and the pathogenesis of heart failure (HF).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the impaired renal mechanosensy responses in CHF are due to ANG-II mediated inhibition of PGE2-mediated release of substance P, which leads to impaired reflexes that contribute to the sodium retention in CHF.
the renal mechanosensor nerve activity in CHF rats was impaired due to ANG-II inhibiting PGE-mediated release of substance P in the renal pelvis.
the responsiveness of renal pelvic mechanosensory afferents is impaired in rats with CHF due to endogenous ANG II inhibitory action on PGE( 2)-mediated neuropeptide release.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the impaired responsiveness of the renal mechanosensors is caused by the increased ANG II, which inhibits the PGE(2)/substance P pathway.
the renal mechanosensensory nerve reflex is suppressed in CHF due to ANGII-mediated inhibition of substance P release from renal pelvic nerves.
the renal mechanosensensory nerves in the CHF rats are impaired due to ANGII-mediated inhibition of PGE2-mediated release of substance P in the renal pelvis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ANG II impairs renal mechanosensensation in CHF.
renal pelvic pressure is not a major determinant of sodium excretion in CHF.
ANG II inhibits PGE(2)/substance P signaling in renal pelvic nerves, leading to impaired responsiveness of these nerves in CHF.
